claims.text: The exceptional ethanol oxidation performance is governed by strong metal-support interactions between Pt nanoparticles and a reducible TiO2 support.
Oxygen vacancies in TiO2 shift the d-band center of supported Pt.
The oxygen-vacancy-induced d-band shift optimizes adsorption and desorption energetics of key ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Optimized intermediate adsorption and desorption improve catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability.
Complete ethanol oxidation is a 12-electron process.
Pretreating TiO2 at 300–400 °C will induce a controlled density of oxygen vacancies.
Replacing carbon with oxygen-deficient TiO2 will enhance electronic interactions between the support and Pt.
Pt supported on carbon lacks the proposed oxygen-vacancy-induced metal-support interaction.
The altered Pt electronic structure modulates the adsorption strengths of ethoxy and acetaldehyde intermediates.
Changes in intermediate adsorption strength affect ethanol oxidation kinetics and product distribution.
The proposed metal-support interaction improves durability by minimizing Pt nanoparticle sintering and agglomeration during operation.
Pt on pretreated TiO2 will show an earlier ethanol-oxidation onset potential than Pt on carbon.
Pt on pretreated TiO2 will show distinct in situ spectroscopic signatures consistent with altered intermediate adsorption energetics.
Pt on pretreated TiO2 will exhibit less nanoparticle agglomeration during extended operation than Pt on carbon.
The proposed benefits will be most pronounced when TiO2 retains the oxygen vacancies produced by the 300–400 °C pretreatment.
Large deviations in temperature or environment may attenuate or eliminate the proposed mechanism.
Support conductivity and surface-area changes may contribute to observed performance independently of the proposed d-band mechanism.
